title: The awaiter pattern
sub: What the compiler turns every await into
cards/0/body:
The compiler doesn't know the word "task". When it sees await x, it expands it into the calls shown below:

  • x.GetAwaiter() gets the waiting object, the awaiter;
  • awaiter.IsCompleted asks whether it's already done;
  • if not, awaiter.OnCompleted(continuation) says "call me when it's ready". The method returns and the thread is free;
  • once it's ready, awaiter.GetResult() takes the result or throws the exception.

The compiler looks up GetAwaiter, IsCompleted and GetResult by name, with no interface involved, and GetAwaiter may even be an extension method. The awaiter itself, however, must implement the INotifyCompletion interface, which declares OnCompleted. Task awaiters also implement ICriticalNotifyCompletion with its UnsafeOnCompleted method, and that's what the generated code subscribes through (in the next lesson you'll see it as AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted).
cards/1/q: Match each awaiter-pattern member to its role
cards/1/pairs/2/1: What to call when it's done
cards/1/pairs/3/1: Take the result or the exception
cards/2/explain: First the awaiter, then the readiness check. Subscribing happens only if it isn't ready.
cards/3/q: What must an awaiter type implement for the compiler to accept await?
cards/3/options/0: The INotifyCompletion interface with its OnCompleted method
cards/3/options/1: Nothing: all awaiter methods are looked up by name only
cards/3/explain: GetAwaiter, IsCompleted and GetResult are looked up by name. Subscribing to completion goes through the INotifyCompletion interface. TaskAwaiter is a struct, so nothing can derive from it.
cards/4/title: Your own awaitable in two lines
cards/4/body: Since GetAwaiter is looked up by name, you can add it to someone else's type as an extension method. For example, to TimeSpan: have it return the awaiter of a Task.Delay task, and you can await a span of time directly.
cards/5/options/0: TimeSpan has a GetAwaiter extension method, and it returns the TaskAwaiter of a Task.Delay task
cards/5/options/2: await can wait on any type without extra code
cards/5/explain: The compiler looks for GetAwaiter the same way foreach looks for GetEnumerator, so an extension method counts. The TaskAwaiter of the Task.Delay task does the rest.
cards/6/body:
A faulted task keeps its exceptions as a list inside an AggregateException. .Result hands you the whole wrapper. A task awaiter's GetResult() behaves differently: it throws the first exception in the list and keeps its original stack trace.

It is GetResult that throws the exception after an await. That's why after await you catch the FormatException itself, not an AggregateException. You can call the same GetResult without await too: t.GetAwaiter().GetResult().
cards/6/code:
Task<int> t = ParseAsync("x");      // the task faulted with FormatException
int a = t.Result;                    // AggregateException with FormatException inside
int b = t.GetAwaiter().GetResult();  // FormatException itself, original stack
int c = await t;                     // same as GetResult
cards/7/q: A task faulted with FormatException. What does its awaiter.GetResult() do?
cards/7/options/0: Throws the FormatException itself with its original stack
cards/7/options/1: Throws an AggregateException with the FormatException inside
cards/7/options/2: Returns default and records the error in the task
cards/7/explain: .Result throws the AggregateException wrapper. GetResult (and therefore await) throws the task's first exception as is.
cards/8/body:
Task.Yield() returns an awaitable whose awaiter always answers IsCompleted = false. So await is guaranteed to suspend the method, and the continuation is queued: in a window, to the UI thread's queue; in a console app, to the thread pool.

Why: to hand the caller a Task right now and run the rest of the method later. Note that Yield doesn't move work to the background. In a window the UI thread still runs the rest, just a bit later. For background work you need Task.Run.
cards/8/deep: In WPF the continuation after Yield goes to the Dispatcher queue with a priority higher than input, so a loop like while (…) { Work(); await Task.Yield(); } doesn't make the window responsive. In Unity the continuation queue is drained once per frame, and anything queued while it is being drained waits for the next frame. So a Yield loop there runs roughly one iteration per frame, but the exact moment depends on the frame phase; to wait for a frame, Unity has its own tools (see the Unity unit).
cards/9/q: What can you await? Select all that apply.
cards/9/options/3: A TimeSpan with a GetAwaiter extension method written for it
cards/9/options/4: An int with no GetAwaiter of its own
cards/9/explain: Everything except int has a GetAwaiter, either its own or an extension method. await needs nothing more.
cards/10/options/0: To guarantee the method suspends: the caller gets a Task immediately and the rest runs later from the queue
cards/10/options/2: To move the rest of the method to a background thread, even in a WPF window
cards/10/explain: Yield's awaiter always answers IsCompleted = false. In a window the same UI thread runs the rest, just later: Task.Run gives you a background thread, Yield doesn't.
